title: Flush alignment and proxy spectral bench - notes and reproductions
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures an exploratory benchmark and profiling run that attempts to isolate latency amplification when client flushes are not aligned with proxy egress pacing. The framing is: small, periodic application-level flushes (e.g., token-at-a-time, streaming partials) interact with proxy buffers and transport scheduling to produce a spectrum of microburst patterns which amplify tail latency and increase p99 token delivery time.

High-level hypothesis:
- When client->proxy flushes have periodic timing (fixed interval or quasi-periodic), proxy egress pacing and the kernel TCP sender can fall into phase relationships that cause packet bunching at egress or larger-than-expected queuing delays inside the proxy.
- The spectrum (frequency content) of flush intervals maps to observed latency amplification; certain harmonics with proxy flush/drain periods cause worst tails.
- Simple mitigations (small random jitter on client flushes, adaptive coalescing at proxy, or modest socket buffer tuning) reduce p95/p99 while keeping p50 unchanged.

Testbed summary:
- Client harness: go-streamer v0.13 (internal), single-threaded event loop to control flush patterns; option to include jitter and to vary message size and inter-flush interval.
- Proxy: edge-proxy v2.9 (C++), default buffering enabled (SO_SNDBUF default, internal 64KB ring buffer for HTTP/2 multiplexed streams).
- Backend model server: runtime-inference v2027.05 on a single A10G-equivalent node (simulated model; token RT ~2ms baseline).
- Network: colocated within same AZ, 25Gb connectivity, simulated link delay 1ms using tc netem for some runs.
- Tools: tcpdump/pcap, tshark, BPF hist (internal) to produce inter-packet gap (IPG) histograms, go bench harness logs, and Prometheus scrape for proxy queue depth metrics.

Key experiment knobs:
- flush_interval_ms: 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100
- flush_pattern: periodic, jittered (uniform +-20%), poisson (mean equal to flush_interval)
- transport: HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2 frames, gRPC (HTTP/2 with flow control on)
- Nagle/TCP_CORK: on (default) vs disabled (TCP_NODELAY set by client)
- proxy_coalesce_ms: 0, 2, 5, 10  (proxy internal timer to coalesce small writes)
- sndbuf: default (system), 64KB, 256KB
- CC algorithm: cubic vs bbr (kernel toggled for controlled experiments)

Reproduction commands (short):
- Start pcap capture on proxy egress: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w proxy-egress.pcap port 443
- Run go-streamer (periodic flush every 5ms): ./go-streamer --target https://edge-proxy:443 --pattern periodic --interval-ms 5 --messages 10000 --concurrency 1
- Collect BPF hist: sudo ./bpf/ipg_hist --iface eth0 --filter "tcp and host modelserver" --out ipg-5ms.txt --window 60
- Run ghz for gRPC path: ghz --proto api.proto --call API.Streaming --insecure --concurrency 1 --rps 100 --data-stream --duration 60s

Representative raw observations (periodic, no jitter, HTTP/2, proxy_coalesce_ms=0):
- flush_interval 1ms: p50=8ms, p95=48ms, p99=158ms, mean throughput=1800 tokens/s
- flush_interval 5ms: p50=11ms, p95=64ms, p99=320ms, mean throughput=1720 tokens/s
- flush_interval 20ms: p50=18ms, p95=80ms, p99=420ms, mean throughput=1500 tokens/s
Notes: p99 grows non-linearly with interval; worst cases showed long (>200ms) gaps between packet bursts in pcap corresponding to proxy internal drain cycles.

When client jitter applied (uniform +-20%):
- flush_interval 5ms (jittered): p50=10ms, p95=30ms, p99=62ms. Throughput unchanged.
- IPG histograms show flattened spectrum: previous strong peak at ~5ms vanishes, energy spreads across frequencies.

Proxy coalescing enabled (coalesce_ms=5) with periodic client flush 5ms:
- p50=12ms, p95=36ms, p99=95ms. Slightly larger p50 but much improved p99 vs no coalesce.

Nagle vs NoDelay:
- With TCP_NODELAY (client sets), p99 reduced modestly for very small messages but increased when proxy coalesce enabled (because kernel schduling produced more syscalls).

gRPC vs HTTP/2 vs HTTP/1.1 chunked:
- gRPC (with HTTP/2 flow control): p99 worse than raw HTTP/2 frames in some configs because flow-control windowing + proxy multiplexing created contention between streams; p95/p99 improved when proxy tracked per-stream backlog and paused reads on hot streams.
- HTTP/1.1 chunked elongated the tail in high-concurrency tests, likely due to connection reuse scheduling and backend serialization.

Spectral analysis notes (BPF IPG hist -> FFT):
- For periodic client flushes, IPG FFT shows a sharp peak at flush frequency and harmonics; proxy queues show correlated energy at harmonic frequencies corresponding to internal drain timer.
- Worst p99 runs had strong harmonic alignment between client flush frequency and proxy timer frequency (proxy_coalesce_ms or internal ring drain period).
- Jitter removes sharp spectral peaks and reduces peak amplitudes by up to 8-12dB in the IPG FFT which correlates with p99 improvements.

Profiling inside proxy (samples and flamegraphs):
- Top CPU time: write aggregation loop (35%), buffer-copy into egress ring (20%), TLS write path (18%), epoll wakeups (12%).
- When microbursts occur, TLS write retries and partial writes spike leading to more epoll events and kernel scheduler transitions; this amplifies end-to-end latency.

Actionable mitigations tried and results:
1) Client-side jitter (cheap): uniformly randomize inter-flush +-20%
   - Pros: large p99 improvement, zero infra change, trivial in SDKs.
   - Cons: nondeterministic ordering of tokens in pathological streaming use-cases.
2) Proxy adaptive coalescing: dynamic timer that coalesces small writes when queueing is below SLO threshold.
   - Pros: reduces syscalls and flattens spectral peaks.
   - Cons: increases p50 slightly; requires careful tuning per model workload.
3) Increase socket sndbuf to 256KB and tune epoll batch sizes.
   - Pros: reduces partial writes and TLS retry storms.
   - Cons: increased memory footprint, risk of larger queuing.
4) Expose SDK knob to switch TCP_NODELAY on/off based on payload size.
   - Pros: fine-grained control.
   - Cons: developer-facing complexity.

Recommended short-term rollout:
- Add optional jitter to hosted SDKs for streaming calls (default off, opt-in for 0.5 initial) and measure production p99 uplift on a few beta customers.
- Implement a small adaptive coalescing prototype in edge-proxy behind a feature flag; metricize queue depths and p99 latency.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How does congestion control (BBR vs Cubic) interact with these microburst patterns under real client concurrency footprints? We only toggled kernel CC in isolated runs; need larger scale tests.
- Do TLS record sizing strategies (force 16KB frames vs small records) change harmonic interactions? Measure with OpenSSL record sizing overrides.
- Can we build an online detector (BPF in proxy) to identify harmful spectral peaks and auto-enable jitter/coalesce?

Quick reproduction checklist for SRE/bench team:
- Deploy bench harness to bench cluster with proxy v2.9+ and model stub that waits 2ms per token.
- Run fixed periodic flush at 5ms, capture proxy-egress.pcap and run ./scripts/ipg_fft.py proxy-egress.pcap to view spectrum.
- Toggle client jitter and proxy_coalesce_ms and compare p95/p99 from Prometheus.

Raw artifact locations:
- pcap: s3://bench-archives/flush-spectral/jun15/ (proxy-egress.pcap, client.pcap)
- BPF IPG outputs: s3://bench-archives/flush-spectral/jun15/ipg-*.txt
- Flamegraphs: https://artifacts.redwood-internal/fg/flush-spectral-20270615.svg

Conclusion:
Small, periodic application-level flushes can interact with proxy and kernel egress scheduling to produce harmonic microbursts that amplify tail latency. Low-effort mitigations (client jitter, modest proxy coalescing) are effective in reducing p99 at negligible throughput cost. The spectral framing proved useful in explaining non-linear increases in p99 and provides a diagnostic path (IPG FFT) that SRE and bench engineers can use to detect problematic flush frequencies.

Notes-to-self:
- Add an experiment where client uses increasing randomness and measure tradeoff curve (p99 vs jitter intensity).
- Run a 72-hour smoke in staging with SDK jitter on for one customer cohort and compare error budgets.
